title: Cold Open: The Workflow Engine Wearing a Model's Name
script: Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 today, and the most load-bearing sentence in the announcement isn't about the model — it's about the harness. The Fable 5 launch landed June 9, 2026: ten dollars in, fifty dollars out per million tokens, included on Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans through June 22. Anthropic's own duration claim is harness-framed: run Claude Fable 5 in an agent harness like Claude Code, and it can work for days — planning across stages, delegating to sub-agents, checking its own work. The autonomy verbs belong to the harness, not raw model output. A May 2026 paper measured it: harness-induced variance in agent benchmarks runs 7.8 times larger than model-induced. Same Claude Opus 4.5: 45.9 percent on SWE-bench Pro under the standardized SEAL scaffold, 55.4 percent under Claude Code. A 9.5-point swing, zero model change. Long-horizon autonomy isn't in the weights. It's AI agent orchestration — and this episode has the receipts: a million-line codebase nobody hand-wrote, the enforcement primitives Anthropic just shipped, a bash loop that throws memory away on purpose, and how to run your first unattended loop this week.

title: The Thesis: The Prompt Is Not the Program
script: Everyone is tuning the wrong layer. METR's February thirteenth numbers: Codex CLI beat their simple Triframe loop in fourteen point five percent of bootstrap samples on GPT-5; Claude Code beat plain ReAct fifty point seven percent with Opus 4.5 — a coin flip, neither statistically significant. METR's words: they "aren't obviously better than the default scaffolds we use for our agents." Our read, not METR's: the unlock is human-engineered workflow structure. Anthropic defines agent workflows as LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths — five patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Even the simplest, prompt chaining, ships with programmatic checks gating intermediate steps. Berkeley's MAST taxonomy annotated sixteen hundred forty-two traces across seven frameworks: fourteen multi-agent failure modes, failure rates from forty-one to eighty-six point seven percent, roughly forty-three percent system design. One verification step added to ChatDev lifted task success fifteen point six percent. A practitioner analysis puts sixty-four percent of AI pipeline risk at the schema layer — failures that parse without error. Workflows versus prompts, prompt engineering versus orchestration — the prompt is not the program.

title: The Codex Story: OpenAI Productized the Loop
script: OpenAI's own team shipped a million-line codebase with zero lines of manually written code. They call the discipline harness engineering. Three engineers, growing to seven over five months, drove Codex to that million lines across roughly fifteen hundred merged pull requests — three and a half per engineer per day, an estimated one tenth the hand-written time. The trail: GPT-5-Codex, September fifteenth, 2025 — working independently for more than seven hours, fixing its own test failures. Then GPT-5.1-Codex-Max shipped compaction — native training across multiple context windows — and OpenAI reported internal tasks past twenty-four hours. Reality check: METR measured its fifty percent time horizon around two hours forty minutes, versus GPT-5's two hours seventeen. The bridge is the harness. February twenty-third, 2026, OpenAI's dev blog: Codex ran for about twenty-five hours uninterrupted, used about thirteen million tokens, and generated about thirty thousand lines of code — four durable markdown memory files, verification commands after milestones, credit to the loop, not one-shot intelligence. OpenAI named the layer: the Codex harness, the agent loop under every Codex experience — threads you resume, fork, archive. The long-horizon coding agent got productized. The product is the loop.

title: The Fable 5 Story: Anthropic Ships the Enforcement Primitives
script: OpenAI productized the loop. Anthropic shipped the enforcement primitives — and its own launch copy says where the autonomy lives. In the Slay the Spire eval, persistent file-based memory improved Fable's performance three times more than for Opus 4.8 — and it reached the final act three times more often. Two distinct three-times figures, and the memory uplift is harness, not weights. Stripe reports the model performed a codebase-wide migration in a fifty-million-line Ruby codebase in a day — work that would otherwise have taken a whole team over two months by hand. Deterministic control lives in Claude Code hooks: thirty lifecycle events, five handler types. Exit code two is a blocking error — its standard error text feeds straight back to Claude. A stop hook exiting two prevents Claude from stopping entirely, so "when is the agent done" becomes deterministic hook code. Claude Code subagents run in their own context windows with custom system prompts and tool allowlists. Experimental agent teams claim tasks with file locking to prevent race conditions. And task budgets show the model a running token countdown for the whole agentic loop — minimum twenty thousand tokens — so the Fable 5 Claude Code loop self-moderates end to end.

title: Compiled Control Flow: /loop, /goal, and the Ralph Lineage
script: Three vendors just compiled the same technique into their agent products: one line of bash that throws the model's memory away on purpose. Geoffrey Huntley named it Ralph: a bash loop — cat PROMPT dot md into claude code, forever. The ralph loop discards conversation history by construction. Every iteration re-feeds four locked files: PROMPT, the fix plan, the specs, and AGENT dot md, which Ralph self-updates with learnings. Git commits and the codebase are the external memory. Huntley's self-reported math: a fifty-thousand-dollar contract delivered for two hundred ninety-seven dollars; six repos shipped overnight. The rule: one item per loop, because output quality clips between one hundred forty-seven and one hundred fifty-two thousand tokens. Chroma's context rot study tested eighteen models: focused three-hundred-token prompts beat one-hundred-thirteen-thousand-token full prompts on every one. The ralph wiggum technique became a first-class primitive. Anthropic's official plugin runs a stop hook loop that blocks session exit, capped by max iterations, with a hard stop after eight consecutive blocks. Codex goal mode ships a verifiable stopping condition. Gemini's extension thanks Huntley by name. Fresh context agents won. The amnesia was the feature.

title: Schemas as Ledgers: Contracts Between Pipeline Stages
script: Amnesia only works if every handoff is written down. A JSON schema isn't formatting — it's the contract that lets stage two trust stage one without re-reading its work. Adherence is engineering, not a model property: GPT-4's June 2023 checkpoint scored under forty percent on complex schemas, trained GPT-4o hit ninety-three, constrained decoding closed it to one hundred — riding a newer model, granted. Anthropic's structured outputs, generally available for Fable 5, compile schemas into token-constraining grammars: no parse errors, no schema-violation retries, grammars cached twenty-four hours. The Claude Agent SDK extends the JSON schema contract across multi-turn runs: tools mid-run, validated JSON at the end — failure is typed, never free-text garbage. Microsoft's Magentic-One keeps two ledgers: a Task Ledger of facts and plans, a per-step Progress Ledger. Stall counter past two? Re-plan from the ledger. OpenAI's SDK makes agent handoffs typed tool calls: Refund Agent becomes transfer to refund agent, Pydantic-validated before the callback fires. The JSON-hurts-reasoning objection didn't replicate: prompts held equal, structured matched or beat free-form — GSM-8K, point seven eight versus point seven seven. XGrammar makes schema validation for agents near-free, up to one hundred times faster. The contract is cheap. Re-reading stage one is not.

title: The Scoreboard: Workflow Numbers vs the Best Prompt Numbers
script: Harness variance runs 7.8 times model variance — yet the prompt side has receipts. Here's the honest scoreboard. Workflow column: agent reliability math. At 95 percent per step, a 20-step agent's odds are about 36 percent; at 99, about 82; at 100 steps, 99 falls to roughly 37. Compounding error in agents punishes the exponent; prompt tuning nudges the base. Anthropic's C compiler: 16 parallel Claude agents, just under 20,000 dollars, 100,000 lines compiling Linux 6.9. Carlini: the task verifier must be nearly perfect, or Claude solves the wrong problem. Harness-only change: Terminal-Bench 2, 69.7 to 77.0 percent on the same model — GPT-5.4, not Claude. SWE-bench scaffold variation: up to 15 points. Prompt column: OpenAI's three GPT-4.1 instructions lifted internal SWE-bench Verified close to 20 percent; planning alone, 4 percent — behavior contracts inside a harness. Prompt sensitivity to formatting swings up to 76 points on Llama 2 13B, roughly 10 across 53 tasks — older open models. GEPA prompt optimization beats GRPO by 6 percent average, up to 20, with up to 35 times fewer rollouts. Except GEPA is an automated eval loop. The workflow optimizes the prompt.

title: How to Start: Your First Locked Loop
script: Your first long-running agent harness is a bash wrapper, a JSON ledger full of passes false, and a completion promise — start at ten iterations, not fifty. How to run a Ralph loop: snarktank ralph, 20,118 stars — fresh instance, clean context, every iteration; default is ten; when every story hits passes true, it prints the COMPLETE promise and exits. Geocodio's weekend build is the autonomous coding loop tutorial: cat PROMPT dot md piped to claude print, max iterations fifty, agent state files — prd dot json flipping to passes true. Two full apps, Friday 4 p.m. to Sunday evening. Scope it: migrations, refactors, dependency updates, test clean-ups — definition of done stated upfront. Twelve-Factor Agents, 23,200 stars: production agents are mostly deterministic code, LLM steps sprinkled in — three to twenty steps. One practitioner's estimate: a fifty-iteration loop runs fifty to a hundred dollars plus; one dev burned two Claude Max 20x subscriptions — four hundred dollars a month — in a few days. Stay close — Ralph amplifies operator skill. Payoff: one refactor cut a test suite from four minutes to two seconds.

title: Takeaway: Make It Legible and Enforceable
script: When OpenAI's harness team hit failures, the fix was almost never "try harder" — because the prompt is not the program; the workflow is. Engineers asked: what capability is missing, and how do we make it both legible and enforceable for the agent? That's the workflows over prompts takeaway: agent harness design. Project Vend, phase one: Claudius lost money. Phase two's most impactful change: forcing Claudius to follow procedures. Weeks with negative profit margin largely eliminated — now running in three cities. The intelligence-shaped fix, a CEO supervisor agent, had a mixed, possibly negative effect. Toby Ord, on METR's data: the AI agent half-life is measurable — a constant per-minute failure rate, success decaying exponentially with task length. Structure moves the exponent. Mitch Ashley at Futurum: delegate a bounded work block the agent owns end to end, not a prompt. Anthropic agrees: define done as a gradeable outcome rubric — iterate, grade, revise, default three iterations, max twenty. Make the missing capability legible. Make it enforceable. Anthropic says Fable 5 can work for days — and now you know which word in that sentence is load-bearing. The harness.
